paragraphs.context: I am pretty much totally and completely petrified
paragraphs.mainIdea: Auggie starts fifth grade next week and he is very afraid. He has not been to school before because he has had many operations and was often sick.
paragraphs.simple: Next week I start fifth grade. I have never been to a real school, so I am very, very afraid. People think I have not gone to school because of my face. That is not why. It is because of my operations. I have had twenty-seven since I was born. The big ones were before I was four, so I do not remember them. Since then I have had two or three every year. Some were big and some were small. I am small for my age, and doctors never found out some of my health problems. So I was sick a lot. That is why my parents said I should not go to school. I am much stronger now. My last operation was eight months ago. I may not need more for a couple of years.

paragraphs.context: What’s cool about really little kids is that they don’t say stuff
paragraphs.mainIdea: When Auggie was small, meeting new kids was not a problem. Big kids know what they say, and that is hard for him.
paragraphs.simple: When I was little, I did not mind meeting new kids. All the kids I met were little too. Little kids do not say things to hurt your feelings. Sometimes they do say things that hurt, but they do not know what they are saying. Big kids know what they are saying. That is not fun for me. Last year I let my hair grow long. I like that my bangs cover my eyes. It helps me not see the things I do not want to see.

paragraphs.context: I know every brick and every tree trunk and every crack in the sidewalk
paragraphs.mainIdea: Auggie knows his own street very well. The streets near the school feel new and strange to him.
paragraphs.simple: Beecher Prep is only a few blocks from our house. But I have been on that street only a few times. I try not to go where many kids walk around. On our street, everyone knows me and I know everyone. I know every brick, every tree and every crack in the street. I know Mrs. Grimaldi, who is always sitting by her window, and the old man who walks up and down the street whistling like a bird. I know the small shop on the corner where Mom gets our bagels. The women at the coffee shop all call me “honey” and give me candy whenever they see me. I love my part of town, North River Heights. So it felt strange to walk down these streets and feel that everything was new. Amesfort Avenue, a street I have walked down a million times, looked very different. It was full of people I had never seen, waiting for buses and pushing strollers.

paragraphs.context: I hate the way I eat. I know how weird it looks.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Auggie knows the way he eats looks strange because of his mouth. Once he watched himself eat in a mirror.
paragraphs.simple: I hate the way I eat. I know it looks strange. When I was a baby I had an operation to fix the top of my mouth, and I had a second one when I was four. But I still have a hole in the roof of my mouth. I also had a jaw operation a few years ago. I have to chew food at the front of my mouth. I did not know how this looked until I was at a birthday party. One of the kids told the mom of the birthday boy that he did not want to sit next to me. He said I was too messy, with bits of food shooting out of my mouth. I know the kid did not want to be mean. He got into big trouble later, and his mom called my mom that night to say sorry. When I got home, I went to the bathroom mirror and ate a cracker to see how I looked when I was chewing. The kid was right. I eat like a tortoise, if you have ever seen a tortoise eat. Like some swamp thing from long, long ago.

paragraphs.context: how something felt on a scale of one to ten
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mom asks Auggie to say how much something hurts, from one to ten. This began after his jaw operation, when he could not talk.
paragraphs.simple: Mom always asked me how something felt, from one to ten. This began after my jaw operation. I could not talk because my mouth was shut with wire. The doctors took a piece of bone from my hip and put it in my chin to make it look more normal. So I hurt in many places. Mom would point to one of my bandages, and I would hold up my fingers to show her how much it hurt. One was a little. Ten was so, so, so much. Then, when the doctor came to see the patients, she told him what needed to change. Mom got very good at knowing what I was thinking, sometimes.

paragraphs.context: if a Wookiee started going to the school all of a sudden
paragraphs.mainIdea: Auggie says the kids were not mean when they looked at him. He would stare at a Wookiee too, because he would be interested.
paragraphs.simple: I am not saying the kids were being mean. Not once did a kid laugh or make noises or do anything like that. They were just normal dumb kids. I know that. I wanted to tell them that. I wanted to say, it is okay, I know I look strange, take a look, I do not bite. The truth is, if a Wookiee came to our school one day, I would be interested. I would probably stare a little! If I was walking with Jack or Summer, I would probably whisper to them, “Hey, there is the Wookiee.” If the Wookiee heard me say that, he would know I was not trying to be mean. I was only saying that he is a Wookiee.

paragraphs.context: The things we do outlast our mortality
paragraphs.mainIdea: This precept says that people remember us for what we do. What we do is like a monument made of memories.
paragraphs.simple: This precept means that people should remember us for the things we do. The things we do are the most important things of all. They matter more than what we say or how we look. The things we do last longer than our life. They are like monuments that people build for heroes after the heroes have died. They are like the pyramids that the Egyptians built for their kings. But they are not made of stone. They are made of the memories people have of you. That is why your deeds are like your monuments. They are built with memories, not with stone.

paragraphs.context: people were getting used to me, no one would actually touch me
paragraphs.mainIdea: Auggie sees that no one will touch him. In dance class, Ximena Chin was so afraid to be his partner that she made up an excuse.
paragraphs.simple: Not long ago I saw that, even though people were getting used to me, no one would touch me. At first I did not see it, because kids in middle school do not touch each other much anyway. But last Thursday, in dance class, my least favorite class, Mrs. Atanabi, the teacher, tried to make Ximena Chin my dance partner. I have never seen someone have a “panic attack” before, but I have heard about it, and I am quite sure Ximena had one then. She was very afraid, her face went white, and within a minute she was sweating. Then she made up a weak reason: she said she really had to go to the bathroom. In the end Mrs. Atanabi let her off, because she did not make anyone dance together.

paragraphs.context: I’ve gotten used to not bothering Mom and Dad with little stuff
paragraphs.mainIdea: Via has learned to find answers on her own and not to trouble her parents. She feels her bad days are small next to what August has been through.
paragraphs.simple: I have got used to not complaining, and I have got used to not bothering Mom and Dad with small things. I have got used to finding answers on my own: how to put toys together, how to plan my life so I do not miss friends’ birthday parties, how to keep up with my schoolwork so I never get behind in class. I have never asked for help with my homework. I never needed to be told to finish a project or study for a test. If a school subject was hard, I went home and studied it until I understood it on my own. I taught myself how to change fractions into decimals by looking online. I did almost every school project by myself. When Mom or Dad ask how school is going, I always say “good,” even when it has not been so good. My worst day, my worst fall, my worst headache, my worst bruise, my worst pain, and the worst mean thing anyone could say have always been nothing next to what August has been through. I am not saying this to look good. It is just how I know things are.

paragraphs.context: I remember very vividly stepping through the door and seeing August
paragraphs.mainIdea: Via comes home after four weeks away. For one short moment she sees Auggie the way other people see him, and she hates herself for it.
paragraphs.simple: Coming home after four weeks felt very strange at first. I remember very clearly walking through the door and seeing August run over to welcome me home. For a tiny part of a moment, I did not see him the way I have always seen him. I saw him the way other people see him. It was only a flash, an instant while he was hugging me, so happy that I was home. It surprised me, because I had never seen him like that before. I had never felt that way before either, and I hated myself for it the moment I felt it. He was kissing me with all his heart, but all I could see was the spit coming down his chin. And suddenly there I was, like all those people who stare or look away.

paragraphs.context: we circle around him like he’s still the baby he used to be
paragraphs.mainIdea: Via says her family treats Auggie like a baby and changes plans because of his moods. She thinks he must grow up, and that he is not normal.
paragraphs.simple: I wish I could ask him these things. I wish he would tell me how he feels. He was easier to read before the operations. When his eyes got small, he was happy. When his mouth went straight, he was playing a trick. When his cheeks shook, he was about to cry. He looks better now, for sure, but the signs we used to read are all gone. There are new ones. Mom and Dad can read every one. But I cannot keep up, and part of me does not want to keep trying. Why can’t he just say how he feels, like everyone else? He does not have a breathing tube in his mouth now that stops him from talking. His jaw is not shut with wire. He is ten years old. He can use words. But we move around him as if he were still the baby he used to be. We change plans, go to plan B, stop conversations, and break promises because of his moods and what he wants and needs. That was fine when he was little. But now he needs to grow up. We need to let him, help him and make him grow up. We have spent so much time trying to make August think he is normal that he really thinks he is normal. And the problem is, he is not.

paragraphs.context: I’m always going to be the sister of a kid with a birth defect
paragraphs.mainIdea: Many people in Via’s new school did not know about Auggie. Via will always be his sister and that is fine, but she does not want to be known only that way.
paragraphs.simple: But in middle school many people did not know about August. My old friends did, but my new friends did not. Or if they knew, it was not the first thing they knew about me. Maybe it was the second or third thing they heard. “Olivia? Yes, she is nice. Did you hear she has a brother who is deformed?” I always hated that word, but I knew it was how people described Auggie. I knew these talks probably happened all the time where I could not hear them, every time I left the room at a party, or met a group of friends at the pizza place. That is okay. I will always be the sister of a kid with a birth defect. That is not the problem. I just do not always want people to know me that way.

paragraphs.context: Not one person in the exotic mix of my family gene pool
paragraphs.mainIdea: Nobody in Via’s family has shown signs of what August has. Doctors said it comes from genes, and both her parents carry the changed gene without showing it.
paragraphs.simple: No one in my big, mixed family has ever shown any signs of having what August has. I have looked for a long time at old, grainy brown photos of dead relatives in head scarves; black-and-white photos of faraway cousins in white suits, soldiers in uniform, ladies with tall hair; and photos of teenagers in wide trousers and long-haired hippies. I never found even a small trace of August’s face in their faces. Not one. But after August was born, my parents got advice about genes. They were told that August had a type of condition that doctors had not known before. It has a very long science name. Sometimes these changes in the genes happen during pregnancy. Sometimes they come from one parent who has the dominant gene. Sometimes many genes and the world around us work together. This is called multifactorial inheritance. In August’s case, the doctors found one of the small changes that did harm to his face. The strange thing is that both of my parents have that changed gene, but you would never know by looking at them.

paragraphs.context: I like how words you don’t understand explain things you can’t understand
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doctors draw little squares to explain genes, but their science cannot be sure. Via likes how the science words sound.
paragraphs.simple: Many, many doctors have drawn little square boxes for my parents over the years to explain the luck of genes. These boxes, called Punnett squares, show which genes pass on and how likely that is. But doctors do not know everything. They can say what is likely, but they cannot promise. They use big science words like “germline mosaicism” or “delayed mutation” to explain why their science is not exact. I actually like how doctors talk. I like the sound of science. I like how words you do not understand explain things you cannot understand. Many, many people are hidden under words like these. Many babies will never be born, like mine.

paragraphs.context: it may have been too much to ask of our children
paragraphs.mainIdea: In her letter, Julian’s mother wonders if too much pressure made Jack hit Julian. She also asks why the school let the new boy in.
paragraphs.simple: I wonder if Jack’s violent act, which no one expected, came from too much pressure on his young shoulders. I mean the new child with special needs who Jack and Julian were both asked to “befriend.” Now that I have seen the child at school events and in class pictures, I think it was too much to ask of our children. When Julian said it was hard to be friends with the boy, we told him he was “off the hook” in that case. We think the move to middle school is hard enough without more heavy duties for these young minds. As a member of the school board, I was also a little upset that the school did not think more about this when the child applied. Beecher Prep is not an inclusion school, which is a school that teaches all kinds of children together. Many parents, including me, ask why this child was let into our school at all. At the least, I am worried that he did not have to meet the same hard rules, such as an interview, as the other new middle-school students.

paragraphs.context: there was no “clean slate” when I went back to school in January
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack goes back to school and finds that his classmates are cold to him. Even Amos and Henry will not talk to him.
paragraphs.simple: Despite what Mr. Tushman said, there was no “clean slate” (a new start) when I went back to school in January. Things were very strange from the moment I got to my locker. I am next to Amos, who has always been an honest kid. I said, “Yo, what up?” and he just gave half a nod, closed his locker door and left. I thought, that was strange. Then I said, “Hey, what up?” to Henry. He did not even try a half smile. He just looked away.

paragraphs.context: I just couldn’t bring myself to sit with him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack knows Auggie will have no one to sit with, but he does not sit with him. He wants some normal time with other kids.
paragraphs.simple: I saw Auggie go into the cafeteria in front of me. I knew he would have no one to sit with. But I could not make myself sit with him. We had been together all morning because we had many classes together. I just wanted a little normal time to relax with other kids. When I saw him go to a table on the other side of the lunch counter, I chose a table as far away as I could find. I sat with Isaiah and Luca, although I had never met them. We talked about baseball the whole time, and I played basketball with them at recess. After that, they were my lunch table.

paragraphs.context: it takes care of its most fragile creations in ways we can’t see
paragraphs.mainIdea: Justin thinks about luck and the world. He believes the world looks after weak things, with the help of people like Auggie’s parents, sister and friends.
paragraphs.simple: My head goes round with this, but then softer thoughts make me feel better, like a soft note in a song. No, no, it is not all luck. If it was really all luck, the universe would leave us completely. But it does not. It looks after its most delicate creations in ways we cannot see. For example, with parents who love you without seeing any fault. And a big sister who feels guilty for being a normal person because of you. And a little boy with a rough voice whose friends have left him because of you. And even a girl with pink hair who carries your picture in her wallet. Maybe it is a lottery, but the universe makes it all even in the end. The universe takes care of all its birds.
hardWords: flatted third on a major chord

paragraphs.context: The ocean just wasn’t living inside my head anymore
paragraphs.mainIdea: Auggie tries to say what it was like to hear with hearing aids. The ocean sound in his head was gone, and sounds felt bright.
paragraphs.simple: How can I say what I heard when the doctor turned on my hearing aids? Or what I did not hear? It is too hard to think of words. The ocean was no longer living inside my head. It was gone. I could hear sounds like shiny lights in my brain. It was like being in a room where one of the lights on the ceiling is broken. You do not know how dark it is until someone changes the light, and then you say, wow, it is so bright in here! I do not know if there is a word that means the same as “bright” for hearing, but I wish I knew one, because my ears were hearing brightly now.

paragraphs.context: I’ve never seen Dad cry before, but I saw him cry tonight
paragraphs.mainIdea: Auggie sees his dad cry quietly on the bed. Then he goes to Via’s room, where Mom is lying next to Via, who is also crying.
paragraphs.simple: I have never seen Dad cry before, but tonight I saw him cry. I had gone into Mom and Dad’s room to find Mom and ask her to put me to bed. But I saw Dad sitting on the edge of the bed, taking off his socks. His back was to the door, so he did not know I was there. At first I thought he was laughing, because his shoulders were shaking. But then he put his hands on his eyes and I saw he was crying. It was the quietest crying I have ever heard, like a whisper. I was going to go over to him, but then I thought maybe he was crying so quietly because he did not want me or anyone else to hear him. So I walked out and went to Via’s room. I saw Mom lying next to Via on the bed. Mom was whispering to Via, who was crying.

paragraphs.context: these lies I told, these fictions, did wonders for my popularity
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miranda’s lies about a little brother who was deformed made her popular at camp. The top girls liked her, changed her hair and makeup, and took her out at night.
paragraphs.simple: The strangest thing is that these lies I told did wonders for how popular I was. The other young helpers heard it from the kids at camp, and they loved it. I was never one of the “popular” girls in anything. But that summer at camp, for some reason, I was the girl everybody wanted to be with. Even the girls in bungalow 32 liked me. They were the girls at the top. They said they liked my hair, but they changed it. They said they liked the way I did my makeup, but they changed that too. They showed me how to turn my T-shirts into halter tops. We smoked. We went out secretly late at night and took the path through the woods to the boys’ camp. We spent time with boys.

paragraphs.context: The only time I felt any regret, if you could even call it that
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miranda feels a little sad when Via and Justin take their bows. Then she sees Auggie looking lost in the happy crowd and goes to him.
paragraphs.simple: The only time I felt any regret, if you can even call it that, was at the end of the play, when the actors came out to take their bows. Via and Justin were the last actors to walk out onto the stage, and the audience stood up when they bowed. I admit that made me a little sad and happy at the same time. But just a few minutes later I saw Nate, Isabel and Auggie come backstage, and they all looked so happy. Everyone was telling the actors well done and patting them on the back. It was the wild, noisy time after a play when actors wet with sweat stand very happy while people come to praise them for a few seconds. In that crowd of people, I saw Auggie looking a little lost. I went through the crowd as fast as I could and came up behind him.

paragraphs.context: Most kids have had sleepovers by the time they’re my age
paragraphs.mainIdea: Auggie has never slept at another house, except once at Christopher’s, and that went badly. So he is afraid about the nature trip.
paragraphs.simple: Most kids have slept at a friend’s house by the time they are my age. Many have gone to camp or stayed with their grandparents. Not me. Not unless you count the hospital, and even then Mom or Dad stayed with me all night. I never slept at Tata and Poppa’s house or at Aunt Kate and Uncle Po’s house. When I was very little, it was because of my medical needs. My breathing tube had to be cleaned every hour, and my feeding tube had to be put back if it came out. When I got bigger, I just did not want to sleep anywhere else. Once I almost slept at Christopher’s house. We were about eight and still best friends. Our family visited his house, and we were having such fun playing Legos Star Wars that I did not want to go home. We begged, “Please, can we have a sleepover?” Our parents said yes. Mom, Dad and Via drove home. Christopher and I played until midnight, until his mom, Lisa, said it was time for bed. Then I got afraid. Lisa tried to help me sleep, but I cried that I wanted to go home. At one in the morning Lisa called Mom and Dad. Dad drove all the way back to Bridgeport to get me. We did not get home until three. So my one sleepover, until now, was a bad time. That is why I am a little afraid about the nature retreat.

paragraphs.context: how you could have a night that’s the worst in your life
paragraphs.mainIdea: When Auggie and Jack get back, nobody has noticed they were gone. Auggie finds it strange that his worst night is a normal night for everyone else.
paragraphs.simple: When we got back to our place in front of the movie screen, no one had even noticed we had been gone. Mr. Tushman, Ms. Rubin, Summer and all the other kids were just watching the movie. They had no idea that something bad had almost happened to me and Jack. It is so strange how that can be. You can have the worst night of your life, but for everyone else it is a normal night. On my calendar at home, I would mark this as one of the worst days of my life. This and the day Daisy died. But for the rest of the world, this was just a normal day. Or maybe it was even a good day. Maybe someone won the lottery today.

paragraphs.context: there was a big shift in the way things were
paragraphs.mainIdea: After the night at the nature retreat, everyone knows the story and it grows bigger. Auggie is now known for it, and Amos, Henry and Miles treat him like a friend.
paragraphs.simple: When I went back to school the next day, the first thing I saw was a big change in the way things were. A huge change. A change like an earthquake. Maybe even a change as big as space. Whatever you want to call it, it was a big change. Everyone, not just in our grade but in every grade, had heard what happened to us with the seventh graders. So suddenly I was not known for what I had always been known for, but for this other thing that had happened. And the story got bigger and bigger each time it was told. Two days later, the story was that Amos had a big fistfight with the kid, and Miles and Henry and Jack had hit the other guys too. The run across the field became a long adventure through a corn maze and into the deep dark woods. Jack’s story was probably the best, because he is so funny. But in every story, no matter who told it, two things stayed the same: I was picked on because of my face and Jack stood up for me, and those guys, Amos, Henry and Miles, kept me safe. Now that they had kept me safe, I was different to them. It was like I was one of them. They all called me “little dude” now, even the sports kids. These big guys I hardly knew before would punch me with their knuckles in the hall now.

paragraphs.context: I am charged with writing two commencement addresses
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Tushman says he writes two speeches every year, and now he knows why. He says this age, when children are at the edge between childhood and what comes next, still moves him.
paragraphs.simple: “Every year,” Mr. Tushman said, reading from his notes with his reading glasses down on the tip of his nose, “I must write two speeches for the end of school. One is for the fifth and sixth grade ceremony today. One is for the seventh and eighth grade ceremony tomorrow. And every year I tell myself, let me do less work and write just one speech for both. It seems like it should not be so hard, right? But each year I still write two different speeches, even when I plan not to. This year I finally found out why. It is not only because tomorrow I will talk to older students who have most of middle school behind them, while your middle school is mostly in front of you. No, I think it is more about the age you are right now. This moment in your lives still moves me, even after twenty years with students this age. Because you are at the edge, kids. You are between childhood and everything that comes after. You are changing.

paragraphs.context: it reminds me that we carry with us, as human beings
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Tushman loves the line “kinder than is necessary.” He says kindness is a choice, and he asks how anyone can check it.
paragraphs.simple: Mr. Tushman looked up at the people. “Kinder than is necessary,” he said again. “What a wonderful line, is it not? Kinder than is necessary. Because it is not enough to be kind. One should be kinder than needed. I love that line, that idea, because it reminds me that, as human beings, we have not only the power to be kind, but the choice of kindness. What does that mean? How do you check it? You cannot use a long ruler. As I said just before, it is not like checking how much you have grown in a year. You cannot count it exactly, can you? How do we know we have been kind? What is being kind, anyway?”

paragraphs.context: I felt like I was floating. It was so weird
paragraphs.mainIdea: As Auggie walks to the stage, everyone stands up and cheers for him. It is a standing ovation.
paragraphs.simple: I felt like I was floating. It was so strange. It was like the sun was shining hard on my face and the wind was blowing. As I got closer to the stage, I saw Ms. Rubin waving at me in the front row. Next to her was Mrs. G, who was crying a lot, but from happiness, and she smiled and clapped the whole time. As I walked up the steps to the stage, the most wonderful thing happened. Everyone started to stand up. Not just the front rows, but the whole room got on their feet, shouting and clapping like crazy. It was a standing ovation. For me.

sentences.context: Whatever you’re thinking, it’s probably worse.
sentences.simple: Whatever you imagine, I probably look worse than that.
sentences.grammar: ‘Whatever’ + subject + verb means ‘anything that’: ‘Whatever you’re thinking’ = ‘any picture you have’; ‘probably worse’ shows he thinks the real look is worse than the picture.

sentences.context: if I were ordinary, she wouldn’t feel like she needs to protect me as much
sentences.simple: If I were normal, Via would not feel that she must keep me safe so much.
sentences.grammar: Second conditional: ‘if I were …, she wouldn’t …’ imagines something that is not true, and shows that Via does not see him as ordinary.

sentences.context: the only reason I’m not ordinary is that no one else sees me that way
sentences.simple: The only reason I am not normal is that nobody else sees me as normal.
sentences.grammar: ‘The only reason … is that …’: the ‘that’ clause gives the one reason; ‘that way’ means ‘as ordinary’.

sentences.context: I haven’t gone to school because of the way I look
sentences.simple: People think I have not gone to school because of how I look.
sentences.grammar: Present perfect ‘haven’t gone’ means ‘not up to now’; ‘because of’ + noun gives a reason; ‘the way I look’ means ‘how I look’.

sentences.context: even though Christopher’s the one who moved far away, I still see him more than I see Zachary and Alex
sentences.simple: Christopher is the one who moved far away. But I still see him more than I see Zachary and Alex.
sentences.grammar: ‘Even though’ joins two ideas that seem opposite (he moved away, but I see him more); ‘the one who’ points to a person; ‘more than’ compares.

sentences.context: We can’t just pretend he’s going to wake up tomorrow and this isn’t going to be his reality
sentences.simple: We cannot just act as if he will wake up tomorrow and this will not be his real life.
sentences.grammar: ‘pretend (that)’ + clause means ‘act as if something is true’; ‘isn’t going to be’ talks about the future; the clause shows Mom’s idea that is not true.

sentences.context: Dad answered angrily, but he didn’t even finish his sentence because he saw me in the mirror
sentences.simple: Dad answered in anger, but he did not even finish his sentence, because he saw me in the mirror.
sentences.grammar: ‘didn’t even finish’: ‘even’ shows it is a surprise that he stopped early; ‘because’ + past tense gives the reason.

sentences.context: In hindsight,” sighed Mom, “yes, I guess.
sentences.simple: Looking back now, Mom said with a sigh, “yes, I guess so.”
sentences.grammar: ‘In hindsight’ means ‘looking back at it now, after it happened’; in ‘sighed Mom’ the verb comes before the name, which is common after a quote.

sentences.context: I would have been more nervous about meeting Mr. Tushman if I’d known I was also going to be meeting some kids
sentences.simple: If I had known I would also meet some kids, I would have been more afraid of meeting Mr. Tushman. But I did not know.
sentences.grammar: Third conditional: ‘would have been … if I’d known’ talks about the past and what was not true: he did not know, so he was less nervous.

sentences.context: What’s cool about really little kids is that they don’t say stuff to try to hurt your feelings
sentences.simple: The good thing about very little kids is that they do not say things to hurt your feelings.
sentences.grammar: ‘What’s cool about X is that …’ puts the topic first and means ‘The cool thing about X is that …’; ‘try to hurt’ shows a plan to hurt.

sentences.context: One of the reasons I grew my hair long last year was that I like how my bangs cover my eyes
sentences.simple: One reason I let my hair grow long last year was that I like how my hair in front covers my eyes.
sentences.grammar: ‘One of the reasons … was that …’ gives one reason out of more than one; ‘grew my hair long’ means ‘let my hair grow long’ (grow + object + adjective).

sentences.context: They think I don’t know they’re staring, but I can tell from the way their heads are tilted
sentences.simple: They think I do not know they are staring, but I can tell from how they hold their heads.
sentences.grammar: ‘They think (that) I don’t know …’ leaves out ‘that’; ‘tell from’ means ‘know by seeing a sign’; ‘are tilted’ is passive: heads held to one side.

sentences.context: As soon as we had walked at least half a block
sentences.simple: Right after we had walked at least half a block from the school, Mom spoke.
sentences.grammar: ‘As soon as’ + past perfect (‘had walked’) shows that the walking was finished, and the next action followed at once.

sentences.context: The funny thing is, if he hadn’t put the backpack between us, I most definitely would have offered to help him
sentences.simple: Henry put his bag between us. If he had not, I would for sure have offered to help him.
sentences.grammar: Third conditional: ‘if + had not + verb, would have + verb’ talks about the past and about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: Hey, the truth is, if a Wookiee started going to the school all of a sudden, I’d be curious
sentences.simple: If a Wookiee suddenly started to come to my school, I would be interested. I would probably stare a little.
sentences.grammar: Second conditional: ‘if + past, would + verb’ imagines something that is not real; ‘started going’ is start + -ing.

sentences.context: The things we do outlast our mortality
sentences.simple: What we do lasts longer than our life.
sentences.grammar: ‘The things we do’ is a noun phrase with a short clause and no ‘that’; ‘outlast’ means ‘last longer than’; ‘mortality’ means that we must die.

sentences.context: Only instead of being made out of stone, they’re made out of the memories people have of you
sentences.simple: But instead of being made of stone, they are made of the memories people have of you.
sentences.grammar: ‘instead of’ + -ing names what is not true, and the main clause says what is true; ‘memories people have of you’ leaves out ‘that’; ‘Only’ here means ‘but’.

sentences.context: I’m pretty sure Ximena had a panic attack at that second
sentences.simple: I am quite sure Ximena had a panic attack at that moment.
sentences.grammar: ‘I’m pretty sure (that) …’ gives a strong guess; the simple past ‘had’ shows one moment in the past.

sentences.context: She figured that it had probably ended up in Grans’s attic, and she kept meaning to look for it
sentences.simple: Mom thought it had probably ended up in Grans’s attic. She kept planning to look for it, but by then I had got used to not wearing it.
sentences.grammar: Past perfect ‘had ended up’ shows it happened before ‘figured’; ‘kept meaning to’ means ‘kept planning to (and did not)’.

sentences.context: This isn’t me being noble, by the way: it’s just the way I know it is.
sentences.simple: I am not saying this to look good. It is just how I know things are.
sentences.grammar: ‘This isn’t me being noble’ means ‘I am not trying to look good’; ‘the way I know it is’ means ‘how I know things are’, and the sentence ends without a noun.

sentences.context: I’d never felt what I was feeling before, either
sentences.simple: I had never felt this way before, either.
sentences.grammar: ‘I’d never felt’ is past perfect (before that moment); ‘what I was feeling’ is a noun clause meaning ‘the thing I felt’; ‘either’ ends a negative sentence and means ‘also not’.

sentences.context: we’ve all spent so much time trying to make August think he’s normal that he actually thinks he is normal
sentences.simple: We have all spent so much time trying to make August think he is normal that he really thinks he is.
sentences.grammar: ‘so much … that …’ shows a result; ‘spend time + -ing’ shows how time is used; ‘we’ve spent’ is present perfect, a time up to now.

sentences.context: I just don’t always want to be defined that way
sentences.simple: I do not always want people to know me only in that way.
sentences.grammar: ‘don’t always want’ means ‘do not want it every time’ (not ‘never’); ‘to be defined’ is passive: other people decide how I am known.

sentences.context: since I’d heard him brag to people that he had a “fifteen-year-old who is reading Tolstoy.”
sentences.simple: It was not real fun, because I had heard him say proudly to people that he had a “fifteen-year-old who is reading Tolstoy.”
sentences.grammar: Past perfect ‘I’d heard’ is before the time of the story; ‘heard him brag’ is hear + object + verb with no ‘to’; ‘brag that …’ introduces what he said.

sentences.context: If he wants to dis me, he’s the one who loses—not me.
sentences.simple: If he wants to treat me without respect, he is the one who loses, not me.
sentences.grammar: ‘If + present, present’ states a general fact; ‘he’s the one who loses’ puts stress on ‘he’; the dash adds ‘not me’ as a contrast.

sentences.context: I just couldn’t bring myself to sit with him
sentences.simple: I knew he would have no one to sit with, but I could not make myself sit with him.
sentences.grammar: ‘couldn’t bring myself to + verb’ means ‘was not able to make myself do something I did not want to do’.

sentences.context: you don’t realize how dark it is until someone changes the lightbulb
sentences.simple: When one light in a room is broken, you do not know how dark it is until someone changes the light.
sentences.grammar: ‘don’t realize … until …’ means ‘see it only after’; ‘you’ means ‘anyone’; ‘how dark it is’ is a question-word clause inside a statement.

sentences.context: I heard them both cursing, until my sweatshirt ripped and the first guy yanked me by my arm
sentences.simple: I heard both of them saying bad words, until my sweatshirt tore. Then the first guy pulled me hard by my arm.
sentences.grammar: ‘heard them both cursing’ is hear + object + -ing (the action was going on); ‘until’ marks the time it stopped.

sentences.context: They had no clue how something bad had almost happened to me and Jack
sentences.simple: They did not know that something bad had almost happened to me and Jack.
sentences.grammar: ‘had no clue’ means ‘did not know’; ‘how’ + clause means ‘that it happened’; past perfect ‘had almost happened’ is before the time of the movie.

sentences.context: it reminds me that we carry with us, as human beings, not just the capacity to be kind, but the very choice of kindness
sentences.simple: It makes me remember that, as human beings, we have not only the power to be kind but also the choice of kindness.
sentences.grammar: ‘not just … but …’ joins two things; the words ‘as human beings’ are an extra phrase between commas; ‘carry with us’ means ‘always have’.

sentences.context: Because you’re at the cusp, kids
sentences.simple: You are at the edge of a big change, kids.
sentences.grammar: ‘Because’ starts the sentence but gives the reason for the earlier sentence; ‘at the cusp’ means ‘at the point where one thing changes to another’; ‘kids’ is how he calls the group.

sentences.context: People started applauding before Mr. Tushman’s words actually registered in my brain
sentences.simple: People started to clap before I really understood Mr. Tushman’s words.
sentences.grammar: ‘started applauding’ is start + -ing; ‘before’ + past simple shows what came first; ‘registered in my brain’ means ‘was understood’.
